extracted.intended_audience: writers of historical fiction / novelists seeking authentic historical research
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for novelists on researching, sourcing, and integrating authentic historical detail into fiction without letting accuracy override story and character. Covers where to research, how to evaluate sources, immersion techniques, and how to learn from other writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the historical context (who, what, when, where)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify specific dates and locations to focus your research; determine the major events, how society functioned, class systems, norms, and taboos that shaped the period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deciding the ‘when’ and ‘where’ guides everything from language to societal norms. Gather as much information as you can about events and social norms because they will hugely influence how your characters move within your story world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a timeline of relevant historical milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot relevant historical milestones to map your story against actual events and give a sense of structure and progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timelines help you work from a structured backdrop — whether a dramatic war or a subtle cultural shift — and can form pivot points around which your story revolves. But remember: history should shape, not dictate, your story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance historical accuracy with plot and character development
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sacrifice plot or character development in the service of rigid historical accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While authenticity matters, 'don't sacrifice plot and character development in exchange for rigid historical accuracy.' Use history to inform your story, not to constrain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find reliable sources and evaluate them critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Check an author's credentials, publication date, perspective, potential biases, and the purpose of each source when deciding how much weight to give it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating sources is like being a detective. Remember that no source is perfect; consider perspective and bias when using material for fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a mix of primary and secondary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult primary sources (diaries, letters, photos) for day-to-day insights and secondary sources (scholarly articles, books) for context and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary sources are a goldmine for everyday life details; combining them with secondary analysis gives a well-rounded picture of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immerse yourself in period media and culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Consume fiction, music, films, radio plays, art, and photographs from or about the time to get a feel for what was important and interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural artifacts help you grasp sounds, smells, fashions, and preoccupations of an era — all useful for sensory worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage other historical fiction (read and deep-read contemporaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read books by authors who write about the same time period and do deep readings to see effective techniques and common pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can learn how authors add everyday customs, describe clothing and technology, and represent speech. Deep reading shows what an author does well and what could be improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study authors' notes to learn where liberties are taken
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine author’s notes and acknowledgements to see what historical deviations other writers employ and where they consider liberties acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes can reveal where it’s okay to take liberties and model how other writers strike a balance between accuracy and storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online databases and digitised collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Search JSTOR, Project Gutenberg, the Digital Public Library of America, and similar digital repositories for primary and secondary material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With many documents digitised, online databases offer access to thousands of sources; they are an excellent starting point for background and primary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult libraries and archives (and librarians)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use local/regional libraries, national archives, and university libraries; ask librarians for help locating resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Librarians are valuable research partners. Archives and special collections often hold unique documents not available elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visit museums and use their expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore museum exhibits and collections for artefacts and context; consult museum research departments or experts where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Museums are treasure troves of artefacts; virtual tours can substitute for in-person visits if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with historical societies for localized/specialized information
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical societies often focus on specific periods or locations and may provide access to archives or expert volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They can often access materials not publicly available and may grant supervised access or help locate documents on your behalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-hand accounts and interviews when viable
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct interviews with people who have first-hand experience or deep knowledge of the era (mainly applicable to modern history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-hand perspectives can provide personal detail unavailable in written records, though they are mostly feasible for more recent history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online forums and communities cautiously and verify information
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult Reddit, Facebook groups, and specialist forums to gain insights, rare images, and resource leads from enthusiasts and experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online communities can be invaluable, but members will have differing views; always fact-check information for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine critiques of secondary works to understand bias and oversimplification
rubrics_metrics.description: When using influential secondary texts (e.g., Howard Zinn), investigate the criticisms of those works to learn about oversimplification and perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding where a source is criticized helps you contextualize its viewpoint and use it responsibly in your research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use everyday-life syntheses for worldbuilding detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult works that focus on daily life (e.g., Ian Mortimer's Time Traveler's Guides, Bill Bryson's At Home) to capture food, clothing, housing, and domestic minutiae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books devoted to the minutiae of everyday life are particularly useful for sensory worldbuilding and showing how ordinary settings reflect broader historical forces.
